source.title: Structure tokens sharpen the feature vocabulary of protein language models

page_placements.theme: Conditional cross-model feature sharing and alignment

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present and readable. Figure images are not included, but relevant numerical results are described in the text and figure legends.
record.tranche_reason: Tests sparse-autoencoder feature recovery and biological information in protein language models, extending this kind of representation analysis to a new model setting. It does not test toy-model superposition geometry.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates SAE features using reconstruction, probes, biological annotations, cross-model matching, and causal interventions. Results about attention-head ablations and contact prediction do not measure any listed claim version and are omitted. Results cited from prior studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study applies TopK SAEs to two protein language models, ESM-2 and ESM-3. It reports whether the recovered sparse features are interpretable, GO-enriched and better than random or shuffled controls (V4). It also reports reconstruction completeness and cross-model convergence of features (parts of V5). It does not measure polysemanticity, neuron-level spreading, toy geometry or feature dimensionality.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that SAEs decompose ESM-2 and ESM-3 into interpretable features that share a convergent biological vocabulary (78% vs 14.2% null). Structure tokens sharpen existing sequence-derived features rather than add new ones. Steering and feature circuits place the features in the causal pathway. They also identify a single bottleneck head (L0H7) for structure input.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses TopK sparse autoencoders, functional probes, feature matching, and causal interventions on protein language models. It does not use the toy-model superposition setup or measure overlapping feature directions in an overcomplete network.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported cross-architecture convergence fraction falls from 0.78 on the full dataset to 0.45 under a homology-aware split, as described in Extended Data Fig. 3. Feature interpretation scores also differ between ESM-2 and ESM-3 and between the two language-model judges.

fits_no_version.finding: Features matched across models (r>0.5) retain functional-site probe AUROC 0.925, versus 0.661 for architecture-unique features.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features shared across models carry most task-relevant information.

record.problems: The study analyzes only two protein language models and selected SAE layers; the authors note that multilayer analysis and wet-lab validation remain untested. The homology-aware analysis yields a lower feature-convergence fraction than the full-dataset estimate. Stability across SAE runs and canonicality of the recovered features are not evaluated.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted attention-head ablation, attribution-patching, contact-prediction, and feature-circuit results because they concern structure-processing mechanisms or causal pathways rather than the versions' claims about superposition or SAE feature recovery as model units.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, sparsity transitions or geometry.
All: neuron polysemanticity and capacity competition are not measured.
Whether features are spread across many neurons; polysemanticity of individual neurons; general-purpose language models.
Stability across SAE seeds or runs; dependence on dictionary size (checkpoints at several expansion factors exist but only reconstruction is compared); whether features are canonical within a model.
All: dimensionality of features is not examined.

missing.what: Shuffled SAE features give functional-site AUROC 0.90 (ESM-3) and 0.91 (ESM-2); random projections give 0.50
Convergent-feature fraction under homology-aware 50% identity split: 0.45 vs 0.78 on the full set
Dead features: 39% (ESM-3) and 26% (ESM-2) of the dictionary
Mean enriched GO terms per feature, SAE vs random projection: ESM-3 67 vs 3.1; ESM-2 80 vs 2.3
Reconstruction cosine similarity above 0.9 across expansion factors 4/8 and k 32/64

record.verdict_notes: Inconsistencies in the text: the raw-activation AUROC is 0.94 in the text but 0.95 in the caption. ESM-2's d_sae is given as 10,240 in Methods but '12,288 in each SAE' in Results. The homology-split probing baseline is 0.959 in Extended Data Fig. 3d. The permutation null uses only 10 shuffles. The author consults for Anthropic, which makes one of the two LLM judges. Probe AUROC is weak evidence for V4 because shuffled SAE features nearly match it.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks with more sparse features than dimensions, overlapping near-orthogonal directions, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether neuron polysemanticity results from capacity competition or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.

The study tests SAE-recoverable features in ESM-2 and ESM-3, protein language models; it does not test the claim across general-purpose language models or directly measure features spread across neurons.
The study evaluates reconstruction and functional information captured by SAE features, but does not test feature stability across training runs or whether SAE features are canonical units.
Whether the model's underlying features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional features.
